_comment: The numbers this repository publishes, in one place, with how each was taken.
Read by claimcheck, which started here and now lives at
vendored copy of it, so CI needs no network and this repository keeps its
Before this file the numbers lived in four: README.md, docs/PERFORMANCE.md,
docs/CUDA.md and tools/plot_benchmarks.py, copied by hand and checked by
nobody. Both failure modes had already happened: a stale 6.92x survived in
the README for several commits after the honest number became 5.47x, and
docs/CUDA.md said the best kernel was '1.94x behind cuBLAS' in one paragraph
and 1.21x in its own table, forty lines apart, for weeks.
tools/claimcheck.py  runs in CI. Citations, retired values, derived claims.
Text against data on a checkout: no GPU, no timing,
nothing to flake, so it can block a merge.
tools/check_perf.py  runs locally on the machine below. Re-runs the
benchmarks and compares within each tolerance. Not in
CI on purpose: a shared virtualised runner cannot hold
a timing threshold, and a perf test that fails at
random teaches people to ignore a red CI.
_tolerance_comment: Tolerances are per kind of measurement and each comes from a spread this
repository has already measured, not from whatever makes the run pass.
GPU wall clock      30%.  docs/PERFORMANCE.md records a benchmark sweep
biased up to 1.6x by the card heating up inside
one process. Taken cold and taken after an hour
of work these differ by roughly a third: the
tf32 row measured 1.9 s cold and 2.5 s warm on
the same build the same afternoon.
CPU wall clock      25%.  Runs against whatever else the machine is doing;
the PyTorch CPU row spanned 5.3-6.3 within its
own three runs.
matmul GFLOP/s      10%.  tools/bench_matmul_isolated.* gives one process
per kernel with a settling pause, which is what
the tighter band buys.
ratios              10%.  Numerator and denominator are measured in the
same session and drift together, so the ratio is
steadier than either side of it.
A tolerance wider than the effect being measured would make this check
decorative. These are wide because the measurements are, and the honest
response to that is a stated band, not a tighter one that fails for being
right.
_retired_comment: Numbers this repository used to publish and must not publish again. The
citation check only proves a value is present somewhere in a file, so a file
holding both the new number and the old one would pass it. This is the other
half: every one of these was true once, is not now, and appearing anywhere
in the tree fails the build.
Each says what replaced it, because a bare list of forbidden numbers becomes
unmaintainable the moment somebody wonders whether it still applies.

Never measured on this workload: the engine was rebuilt with /arch:AVX2 and compared in alternating runs, and the two are indistinguishable inside the run-to-run spread. The matmul loop is bound by L1 traffic, not by vector width.
retired.replaced_by: nothing. There is no speedup to report; the entry now says so and keeps the portability argument, which was always the real reason.

retired.was: MNIST on the GPU, in three places in docs/PERFORMANCE.md, one in docs/CUDA.md, the v0.6.0 release page and the repository description -- alongside 23.5 s for the CPU and a 5.5x ratio drawn from the pair. None of the three was ever a value in this file: mnist-engine-cuda went 4.7 -> 4.0 and mnist-engine-cpu has been 24.1 since the file was created. So the flagship document contradicted the flagship claim, in the same repository, for as long as both existed.
retired._why_it_survived: This is the failure claimcheck's own header describes -- 'a document saying 1.94x behind in one paragraph and 1.21x in its own table, forty lines apart' -- and claimcheck did not catch it. It verifies that a claim appears in the files that cite it, and that a retired value appears nowhere. It has no rule against a file containing a *different* number for the same quantity, because it has no idea which numbers describe which quantity. Retiring the value is the fix the tool does offer, and it only works after a human notices.
retired._why_its_companions_are_not_here: 23.5 and 5.5 cannot be retired, and the reason is a real limit worth stating. Retirement matches bare numbers, so 23.5 also matches the legitimate '23.4 s' baseline in the Conv2d table, and 5.5 also matches '0.65 ms of about 5.5 ms' and '5.5-9.5 GB/s' -- three true statements about three other quantities. A retired value is only usable when it does not collide, and this one does not.

claims.how: mnist_demo, 2000-image subset, 12 epochs, 12 threads. Observed 17.6-17.8 over four runs. Re-measured 2026-08-04 in one alternating session with every other MNIST row, after the host buffer pool: comparing a number taken today against one taken on another day is the mistake this file exists to prevent, and the machine was measurably slower today -- PyTorch on CUDA came out at 2.7 s against the 2.1 this file used to carry, on code that had not changed.
claims._tolerance_note: Wider than the GPU rows because it is. The CPU rows run against whatever else the machine is doing, and the original three runs of the PyTorch one spanned 5.3-6.3 by themselves. Holding a number to a band tighter than the spread it was drawn from is a test that fails for being right.
